601.quote_or_event: “The self-willed manmukh is very lazy; he is trapped in the wilderness.”
601.explanation: Guru Nanak names laziness as a mark of the manmukh, the self-willed person, and says it leaves him lost and trapped.
601.tie_back: The Kural says the grime of laziness dims and puts out the lamp of a family; Guru Nanak likewise shows sloth leading to ruin, though of a person's spiritual life rather than a family's standing.
601.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1011, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
601._accuracy_note: Partial: sloth as the road to ruin matches, but the lamp image and the concern for the family line are absent.

602.quote_or_event: “O mind, why are you so lazy? Become Gurmukh, and meditate on the Naam.”
602.explanation: Guru Amar Das challenges the mind's laziness and sets against it the active, Guru-facing life of the gurmukh.
602.tie_back: The Kural tells those who want their family to stand to see laziness for what it is and kill it in their conduct; Guru Amar Das likewise names laziness and answers it with a daily discipline.
602.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 28, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
602._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both condemn sloth and call for disciplined practice, but the Kural's aim is the family's honour and Guru Amar Das's is remembrance of the Name.

603.quote_or_event: “O my foolish and silly soul, why are you too lazy to serve?”
603.explanation: Guru Arjan calls the lazy soul foolish for neglecting service (seva) to the Lord.
603.tie_back: The Kural calls the man who clings to laziness a fool whose family perishes even before he does; Guru Arjan likewise links laziness with folly, though the loss he warns of is spiritual.
603.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1095, Raag Maaroo (Maaroo ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
603._accuracy_note: Reasonable: laziness as folly is a close match, but the Kural's ruin of the family has no counterpart in this line.

604.quote_or_event: “The lustful, the angry, the clever, the deceitful and the lazy waste their lives in slander, and never remember their Lord in meditation.”
604.explanation: Kabir places the lazy beside the lustful, the angry and the deceitful, as people whose lives drain away into faults.
604.tie_back: The Kural says that for those sunk in laziness who make no worthy effort, faults keep multiplying; Kabir likewise counts laziness among the vices that gather together and waste a life.
604.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
604._accuracy_note: Partial: laziness keeping company with other faults matches, but Kabir does not make sloth the cause of the others or speak of the family's fall.

605.quote_or_event: “Wake up, O mind! Wake up! Why are you sleeping unaware?”
605.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur calls the heedless (gaafal) mind out of its sleep.
605.tie_back: The Kural names procrastination, forgetfulness, laziness and oversleeping as the pleasure boat of those bound for ruin; Guru Tegh Bahadur's cry against heedless sleep addresses two of the four, forgetfulness and sleep, directly.
605.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 726, Raag Tilang, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
605._accuracy_note: Reasonable: heedlessness and sleep match two of the Kural's four failings, but the Kural analyses worldly ruin and Gurbani's sleep is spiritual unawareness.

606.quote_or_event: Before his death in 1539 Guru Nanak appointed his devoted disciple Lahina, renamed Angad, as his successor; Angad's loyal conduct had persuaded Nanak that he would be more suitable than either of the Guru's two sons.
606.explanation: At the first Sikh succession, the Guruship passed not by inheritance but to the disciple whose service and obedience had proved him.
606.tie_back: The Kural says those who lack exertion get little good even from a world-ruler's inheritance; the first Sikh succession likewise shows the great prize going to proven devotion rather than to birth.
606.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sikhism: Guru Angad” (W. H. McLeod) (paraphrase)
606._accuracy_note: Partial: the passing over of heirs fits the Kural's point, but Britannica credits Angad's loyalty and does not say the sons were idle, so the sloth element is not attested.

607.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself a guru or a spiritual teacher, while he goes around begging - don't ever touch his feet.”
607.explanation: In the same salok in which he mocks the lazy man who pierces his ears to pass as a yogi, Guru Nanak tells his hearers to deny honour to the idle who live by begging.
607.tie_back: The Kural says the lazy who make no worthy effort will hear rebuke and scorn; Guru Nanak likewise withholds respect from those who will not work.
607.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
607._accuracy_note: Reasonable: loss of respect as the consequence of idleness is shared, though Guru Nanak's target is specifically the idle false holy man.

608.quote_or_event: “Within this body dwell the five thieves: sexual desire, anger, greed, emotional attachment and egotism. They plunder the Nectar, but the self-willed manmukh does not realize it; no one hears his complaint.”
608.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that the five thieves living inside a person rob him while he is unaware, and that no one answers his cry.
608.tie_back: The Kural says laziness in one of noble birth makes him a slave to his enemies; Guru Amar Das likewise shows the unwatchful person plundered by enemies, though they are inner vices, not outside foes.
608.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
608._accuracy_note: Next-best: the unguarded person falling to enemies matches, but sloth is not named here and Sikhism gives no worth to noble birth (kul), which the Kural takes for granted.

609.quote_or_event: “My mind is lazy and sleepy. The Lord, Har, Har, has led me to meet the Holy Guru; meeting the Holy, the shutters have been opened wide.”
609.explanation: Guru Ram Das confesses a lazy, drowsy mind and says that meeting the Guru threw open its closed doors.
609.tie_back: The Kural says the faults of family and manhood vanish once a person throws off the rule of laziness; Guru Ram Das describes the same turn from sloth to openness, though he credits the Guru's grace rather than one's own effort.
609.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 697, Raag Jaithsree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
609._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the reversal of sloth is shared, but Gurbani attributes it to grace and the Guru, while the Kural puts it in the person's own hands.

610.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
610.explanation: In Japji, Guru Nanak tells the yogis that the real conquest is of one's own mind, and that this is the same as conquering the world.
610.tie_back: The Kural promises the tireless king, all at once, the whole world that Vishnu strode across; Guru Nanak also speaks of winning the whole world, but by mastering the mind rather than by conquest.
610.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (Pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
610._accuracy_note: Partial: both promise the world to the one who masters himself, but the Kural's reward is a king's dominion, framed by a Vaishnava allusion Sikhism does not share, while Guru Nanak's is inner victory.
